opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was one of those experiments where I went in expecting one thing and came out with a somewhat humbling lesson. The setup was pretty simple. In the standard AlphaZero-style loop, your training data comes from self-play: the current network plays games against itself, MCTS improves on the raw policy at each move, and you distill those improved search targets back into the network. Everything is on-policy in the sense that the board states you train on are the ones your current policy actually visits.

I wondered whether that was really necessary. If MCTS is a policy improvement operator, why not just sample a bunch of board states from somewhere else, maybe old games, perturbed positions, or fairly random states, rerun the search there to get fresh targets, and train on those? You'd get a lot more coverage of the state space, and in principle the search label is "correct" regardless of how you arrived at the position.

What I found is that it helps much less than you'd hope, and sometimes it actively hurts. Most randomly selected or stale states aren't positions a strong player would ever reach. So you're spending model capacity and gradient updates getting very good at evaluating positions that don't matter, while the positions that matter, the ones on the frontier of your current policy's play, get relatively less attention. The network becomes a decent generalist on weird board states and a worse specialist on the distribution it actually has to play in.

There's also a subtler issue. The quality of the MCTS target depends on the network's value estimates at the leaves. In parts of the state space the network has rarely seen, those value estimates are noisy, so search doesn't magically produce clean labels there. You're bootstrapping off a model in exactly the region where it's least reliable. On-policy data has a self-correcting property: the states you visit are ones where the network gets feedback, mistakes surface in actual game outcomes, and the distribution shifts as you improve.

So the takeaway for me about off-policy learning more broadly was: having a good improvement operator isn't enough. The state distribution you apply it to matters a lot. Off-policy data is valuable when it's near the distribution you care about, like reanalyzing recent games with a stronger network, which is basically what MuZero Reanalyze does and why it works. But "more diverse states" isn't free. Coverage that isn't aligned with where the policy is going is mostly wasted compute, and sometimes it's a distraction.

I think that maps pretty directly onto things like robotics and LLM post-training. People want to throw huge off-policy datasets at the problem, and that helps for pretraining a prior. But for the improvement step, the data that moves the needle is close to what your current policy actually does, because that's where its errors live.

fable-5.1.text:
So the setup was pretty simple. In the normal AlphaZero-style loop, you generate games by self-play, and every position you train on comes from a trajectory the current policy actually produced. What I wanted to know was how much of the learning signal actually depends on that. So instead I took a big bag of board states that were basically arbitrary, some from old games, some from a weaker policy, some just scrambled around, and I reran the search from scratch on each of them and treated the search result as the training target.

The first thing I learned is that it works way better than my intuitions said it should. The search is sort of a local oracle. If you give it a state and enough compute, it gives you back an improved policy for that state, and it doesn't care how you got there. So in that narrow sense the whole thing is off-policy for free, and the data distribution question becomes a question about coverage rather than about correctness. That was kind of a relief, because it means you can decouple "where do I get interesting states" from "how do I label them."

The second thing, which was the more sobering lesson, is that coverage really matters and it's not symmetric. When the states came from a much weaker policy, the network got very good at punishing weak play and then fell apart against itself, because it had never been forced to think hard about positions that only arise when both sides are strong. So the targets were all correct, but the distribution was pointing the model at the wrong part of the space. That's the real content of the off-policy problem for me. It's not that the labels are biased, it's that the question of what to label is itself a policy decision, and if you outsource it to something that's not the thing you're deploying, you quietly get a different objective.

And the third takeaway, which I think generalizes beyond games, is that this is the cleanest version of a thing we keep running into in robotics. If you have an expensive teacher that can grade any state, you can treat data collection as a search over states rather than as rolling out a policy. But you then have to design the state proposal distribution with as much care as you'd design the reward, because that distribution is where all the inductive bias lives. In Go the oracle is MCTS. In robotics it might be a slow planner or a human or a world model, but the structure of the mistake is identical. You can have perfect supervision and still learn the wrong thing by asking about the wrong states.

astra-6.text:
The lesson was that the policy that generates your training positions doesn’t necessarily have to be the policy you’re trying to improve. You can take a board state, run MCTS from it with your current network, and get a fresh training target. Even if that position came from a much older policy, the search is telling you what your current system thinks you should do there.

So there are two things that are easy to conflate: how you get the states, and how you get the targets for those states. You can be off-policy in the first sense while continually improving the second through search.

That doesn’t mean the state distribution is irrelevant. If you never train on positions that matter when your stronger policy plays, that’s still a problem. But it suggests you can get more learning out of revisiting existing experience than you might expect, rather than having to generate a completely fresh batch of games every time your policy changes.

sol-6.1.text:
The surprising thing was how much you could learn without generating fresh on-policy games. You could take a board position from old data, rerun MCTS with the current network, and get a better training target for that position.

So the position can be off-policy, while the search target reflects your current understanding of the game. You’re not just imitating whatever move the old policy happened to make. You’re asking, “Given what I know now, what should I do here?”

That made me appreciate that collecting experience and improving from experience are separable. You can get more learning out of the same states by spending computation on them again. Of course, which states you have still matters—searching old positions doesn’t automatically give you coverage of situations you’ve never encountered.
